title: Computational Identity Algebra
abstract: The field of computer science is rife with notions of "equivalence," yet rarely addresses the fundamental question of what constitutes the "same" computational object. This paper introduces Computational Identity Algebra (CIA), a formal framework designed to rigorously define and analyze identity relationships in computational contexts. CIA provides a mathematical notation, denoted as [ (A, B) ], to represent the identity relation between computational objects A and B. The research presented explores various scenarios, including program modifications, model distillation, and agent replication, to determine whether the objects remain identical after these transformations. The core of CIA rests on establishing a set of axioms and rules governing identity, aiming for a robust and consistent methodology for assessing computational identity. This work lays the groundwork for a deeper understanding of identity in complex computational systems and opens avenues for applications in areas such as software verification, model management, and autonomous agent coordination. ---

title: Anonimização de documentos judiciais e dados sensíveis no Brasil: uma abordagem multidimensional entre o enquadramento jurídico, a evolução da NLP e o paradigma agêntico
abstract: O processamento e a divulgação de documentos no âmbito do Poder Judiciário brasileiro exigem uma constante ponderação entre o princípio constitucional da publicidade dos atos processuais e o direito fundamental à privacidade e à proteção de dados pessoais, assegurado pela Lei Geral de Proteção de Dados Pessoais (LGPD). Este artigo apresenta uma revisão multidimensional e didática das técnicas de desidentificação de textos jurídicos, traçando sua evolução histórica desde as heurísticas baseadas em regras e expressões regulares (RegEx) até o Reconhecimento de Entidades Nomeadas (NER) com aprendizado profundo (como o corpus LeNER-Br) e, finalmente, as arquiteturas baseadas em Modelos de Linguagem de Larga Escala (LLMs) sob o paradigma agêntico. Analisam-se os riscos de vazamento de informações pessoalmente identificáveis (PII) por acúmulo de contexto lateral e injeções indiretas de prompt. Por fim, são apresentadas e demonstradas soluções de referência por meio de três notebooks práticos anexos, abrangendo o Microsoft Presidio adaptado para o português, modelos Transformer baseados em aprendizado profundo e abordagens generativo-agênticas com Large Language Models (LLMs).

title: A survey on Quantum Key Distribution: Foundations and future directions
abstract: Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) is a mechanism for ensuring secure key exchange based on the fundamental principles of quantum mechanics. It has evolved significantly over the past four decades. QKD networks have evolved from experiments to large-scale deployments, enabling longer transmission distances and enhanced security performance. Existing information security relies on modern cryptographic primitives such as Elliptic Curve Diffie–Hellman (ECDH), RSA, and AES. Although AES-256 is considered quantum-resistant, ECDH and RSA cannot withstand attacks by a specific quantum computer. Specifically, with enough quantum bits, Shor’s and Grover’s algorithms can break RSA and ECDH through rapid integer factorization and quantum search capabilities, respectively. Consequently, QKD offers a promising method towards information-theoretic security, using trusted nodes, optical routers, and future quantum repeaters. However, completely replacing current infrastructure with QKD systems is both costly and impractical. Thus, existing QKD can be integrated into current infrastructure, including dark fiber and satellite systems. Previous surveys have primarily focused on isolated aspects such as fiber-based QKD, free-space QKD, or theoretical Internet architectures. There is a lack of a comprehensive survey that simultaneously presents fundamentals, QKD protocols and security, network implementations, and experimental advances. This makes it difficult for readers to grasp the full scope of the field. This survey focuses on QKD from the ground up, covering the essential foundations of QKD, exploring various QKD protocols, concerning different types of attacks, reviewing real-world QKD network deployments, and highlighting challenges and future directions.

title: Explainable Transformer Models for Clinical Prediction Tasks on Structured Electronic Health Records
abstract: Predictive models over structured electronic health records (EHRs) remain central to machine learning for healthcare, but few have jointly emphasized quantitative laboratory information and interpretability with respect to input medical events. We present BERT-LER, a BERT-style model for coded EHR timelines pretrained and fine-tuned from a de-identified EHR dataset of 75 million patients, that encodes laboratory test results as discrete tokens while retaining graded information through percentile-based binning, paired with Integrated Gradients for token-level attributions grounded in the input EHR sequence. We benchmark our approach on the public EHRShot benchmark suite and on an asthma severity progression study based on real-world data. This addresses a methodological gap in EHR foundation-style modeling by unifying laboratory value representation and explainability in a single framework, while assessing whether both predictive performance and explanations generalize beyond standard clinical prediction tasks. Across EHRShot and asthma tasks, BERT-LER achieves predictive performance that is competitive with, and on laboratory-related tasks often exceeds, publicly available benchmark models, and provides attributions that align with clinically known risk factors. Our architecture and explainability approach can be applied to many therapeutic areas and prediction tasks using language models trained on structured EHRs.

title: Break It Down, Pass It On: Cross-Task Skill Transfer in LLM Agents
abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents can induce skills from completed tasks and reuse them later to grow more capable with experience. In practice, induced skills may transfer unreliably and can even harm the agent that retrieves them. When agent-induced skills transfer reliably across tasks remains an open question. We conduct a comprehensive and controlled study of how the way skills are induced shapes their transfer across tasks. Specifically, we compare task-level with subtask-level skill induction and text with code skill formats, the two axes along which existing methods differ. Task-level skills mostly reduce the agent's performance below its no-memory baseline while subtask-level skills raise it above on average, and text skills transfer better than code skills. To further understand our findings, we examine two complementary properties of the induced skills: specificity, which measures how closely a skill matches real tasks, and abstractness, which measures how evenly its relevance spreads across tasks. Neither property alone predicts task success, but their combined effect does, which we propose as a skill utility score. The score correlates consistently with task success when skills are transferred, and subtask-level and text skills score higher. Computing skill utility only needs the skills and task descriptions but not any task execution, so our score serves as a practical diagnostic of a skill memory before any new task runs.

title: DICS: Data-Informed Centroid Splitting for Decision Tree Classifiers
abstract: Decision tree-based models are widely used in machine learning due to their interpretability and strong empirical performance. However, training decision trees can be computationally expensive, particularly for large and high-dimensional datasets, largely due to the exhaustive search over candidate splits at each node. To improve computational efficiency, we propose Data-Informed Centroid Splitting (DICS), a clustering-based framework that constructs a compact and informative set of candidate splits using data-driven priors. By incorporating class-aware structure, DICS significantly reduces the split search space for classification tasks while preserving predictive performance. We further provide theoretical analysis showing that under the stated assumptions, DICS does not degrade the performance of classification trees compared to exhaustive split search. DICS can be incorporated into classification trees, random forests, and gradient-boosting models. Extensive experiments demonstrate that DICS achieves comparable accuracy while substantially reducing training time across synthetic and benchmark datasets, highlighting the benefit of integrating data-informed priors into split selection for scalable classification tree learning.

title: SABET-QA: Temporal Knowledge Graph Question Answering
abstract: Question Answering over Temporal Knowledge Graphs (TKGQA) requires reasoning over time-sensitive facts, yet existing embedding-based methods struggle with multi-step queries due to single-pass reasoning pipelines. We propose SABET-QA, a framework that iteratively refines reasoning states across multiple hops via a bidirectional entity-temporal scoring mechanism and a slot-aware contextualization module that aligns question semantics with temporal KG embeddings. A differentiable working memory enables progressive hypothesis refinement, while auxiliary temporal boundaries serve as coarse supervision when available. Experiments on CronQuestions, Complex-CronQuestions, MultiTQ, and TimeQuestions demonstrate consistent improvements over strong baselines, particularly on complex multi-step temporal queries.

title: Unsupervised Anomaly Detection Using Flow Matching on Tabular Data
abstract: Financial anomaly detection often relies on large unlabeled transaction logs, where anomalous samples may already be present during training. Such training-set contamination violates the clean-normal data assumption underlying many anomaly detection methods. Although flow matching has demonstrated strong performance in generative modeling, its robustness in unsupervised tabular anomaly detection remains underexplored. In this work, we study flow-matching-based anomaly detection under contaminated training data by comparing Time-Conditioned Contraction Matching (TCCM) with Forest-Flow and evaluating multiple anomaly scoring functions. Our results show that the choice of anomaly score is critical. The original single-step Decision score used by TCCM is sensitive to contamination, whereas trajectory-based Deviation and Reconstruction scores provide more stable anomaly signals. With these scores, Forest-Flow becomes competitive with, and in some cases outperforms, TCCM. These findings highlight the importance of anomaly scoring for flow-matching methods in financial anomaly detection under severe class imbalance.

title: Fotonien parametrinen monistaminen Josephsonin parametrisellä muuntimella
abstract: Reading information from a qubit is a foundational operation in quantum computing that commonly involves measuring microwave-frequency photons. Ultrasensitive nanobolometers have recently emerged as promising cryogenic detectors for this task. The observation of even weaker signals could be enabled by cascading a quantum circuit that replicates a received photon into two identical copies, effectively doubling the photon signal over multiple stages. However, implementing such multi-stage duplication without losing signal fidelity remains a major challenge. Here we show that a multiplication circuit implemented with parametrically driven Josephson parametric converters yields perfect photon duplication with a single stage, but degrades upon subsequent iterations. Through numerical simulations, we find that the number of received photons reaches at most 98% of perfect efficiency with two doublings and decreases linearly as a function of the doubling depth. We verify the single-stage perfect multiplication both analytically and via simulation. These results map the performance boundaries of parametric multiplication circuits, expanding the toolkit for amplifying weak cryogenic signals and contributing the development of high-fidelity readout interfaces essential for scalable quantum computing.

title: Which Axiom Seams Yield
abstract: A formal library records which axioms each theorem depends on. Some of those dependencies are removable and some are load-bearing, and the difference is not visible from the dependency graph. Deciding whether an axiom is worth attacking by attacking it costs days per axiom. Two measurements, both computable in seconds from the library text, predict the answer. The guard ratio — the proportion of an axiom's dependency cone already carrying an explicit "avoids this axiom" annotation — measures how much of the seam previous contributors have removed. The consumer profile — whether the theorems that invoke the axiom consume a general lemma while holding a stronger hypothesis, or construct an object the axiom exists to produce — measures whether what remains is removable at all. Three seams in set.mm were worked to completion under this framework. ax-13 has a guard ratio of 0.751 and yields nothing: 371 of its 494 reaching theorems already carry guards, and 150 further theorems exist solely as distinct-variable variants of ax-13-dependent statements. ax-cc has a guard ratio of 0.003 and also yields nothing, for the opposite reason: of 1,011 theorems reaching it, 20 invoke a countable-choice principle directly and each of the twelve mathematical ones constructs a sequence from pointwise existence. ax-ac has a guard ratio of 0.128 and yields substantially. The ax-ac yield concentrates in a single defect class. Three general domination lemmas — fodomg, fnrndomg, imadomg — have 20 direct callers between them. Nine of those callers already hold a well-orderable domain and do not use it. Severing those nine edges removes 208 of the 546 theorems from the choice cone, including bayesth, eulerpart, totprob, caratheodory, and the entire smf and von families. Seven repairs have been constructed, six submitted to metamath/set.mm, and one merged. A census of every $j usage … avoids directive in set.mm is reported: 3,113 axiom-guard pairs over 1,133 theorems.

title: Universal Computational Lagrangian
abstract: This paper introduces the Universal Computational Lagrangian (UCL), a novel theoretical framework designed to unify classical mechanics with computational algorithms. The core principle of the UCL is that the minimum action path, derived from the principle of least action, directly translates into a computable algorithm. This eliminates the need for traditional variational methods and allows for the direct computation of trajectories based on the system's Lagrangian. The UCL proposes a 'Computation Action' concept, and outlines how training, search, and planning processes can be formulated as variations of this action. This framework provides a foundation for developing intelligent systems capable of dynamically adapting to complex environments. The key mathematical concept underpinning this approach is the representation of physical systems as algorithms, and the application of computational techniques to solve classical mechanics problems. The paper outlines the theoretical underpinnings and suggests potential avenues for future research.

title: From an Evidence-Bound Knowledge Graph to Serial Fiction
abstract: This paper presents MOBOT, an autonomous, provenance-preserving world-expansion engine that incrementally constructs a temporal knowledge graph and ontology from an evidence stream, and a pilot application that derives serial fiction from the resulting world library. The central research question is not whether a language model can write a single plausible story. It is whether a continuously expanding, contested, and partially uncertain information world can become reusable narrative infrastructure for novels, games, financial scenarios, simulations, and other media without copying its surface subject matter or granting a model authority over canonical data. MOBOT begins with an event node and grows through bounded discovery, source staging, exact-span extraction, event-identity review, ontology adjudication, and guarded canonical import. Adopted events and relations are only one part of the library. The system also preserves observations, rejected or unadopted articles, exploration attempts, model and rule decisions, revisions, and the reasons why a relation was accepted, deferred, or rejected. A separate Narrative Derivation Engine reads immutable snapshots of this library and converts graph-growth dynamics into a narrative intermediate representation called a *growth packet*. Each packet binds one primary event to relevant relations, observations, negative-space evidence, work patterns, and literary features such as mood, energy, motif, narrative motion, and relationship dynamics. It then produces exactly one causally connected episode under a typed episode contract. As of the evaluated snapshot on 20 August 2026, the MOBOT source bundle contained 87 public event nodes, 86 supported relations, 224 observations, 12,647 literary/work traces, and 10 recurring work patterns. The narrative database contained three public serials, 31 chapters, 31 recursively linked growth packets, and 88 source bindings. Twenty newly generated pilot chapters were automatically checked for minimum prose length, source relevance, timestamp correctness, continuity fields, and leakage of JSON or internal editorial metadata; all 20 passed these structural checks. These figures establish implementation feasibility and provenance coverage, not literary superiority. No controlled reader study has yet established entertainment quality. The contribution is a compact architecture in which evidence acquisition, canonical world state, narrative transformation, and public prose remain separate. SQLite is authoritative; model output is a typed proposal; Rust performs validation and the only accepted writes; public prose is a derived artifact with explicit fictional disclosure. The paper describes the architecture, data model, validation contract, pilot deployment, limitations, and a research agenda for evaluating narrative quality and extending the engine to other media. **Keywords:** knowledge graph, ontology, provenance, temporal world model, autonomous agents, computational narrative, story generation, grounded generation, serial fiction, event sourcing, human–AI co-creation

title: PRE-GHR XL: The Mathematics of the Gap — Entropy-Weighted Residue and Violation Budgets
abstract: The residue δ₀ of XXXVIII/XXXIX counts what must remain — the minimal number of trace units any admissible reconstruction is forced to retain. This paper asks a different question: how much of what remains matters. It develops δ₀^(w), the minimal weighted residue under an admissible weight class, and separates it from the violation budget B — how far practice may drift from the ideal before the budget is exceeded — which lives on the governance layer and is a regime choice, not a consequence of the protocol. The contribution is inheritance, not invention: the paper proves which parts of the XXXIX property layer survive the move from counting measures to non-negative additive set functions, item by item, with each migration condition stated. title: Beyond the Black Box: Clinically Engineered Features and a Composite Risk Score for Diabetes Readmission Prediction
abstract: Hospital readmission among patients with diabetes remains an important clinical and economic challenge, yet predictivemodelling research often emphasises algorithmic solutions over clinically grounded feature derivation.This study developed and evaluated a systematic, interpretable feature-engineering framework for stratifying diabetes readmission risk using noninvasive administrative and clinical data extracted from electronic health records.The analysis used 40,000 encounters from the Diabetes 130-US Hospitals dataset.Twenty engineered predictors were derived across seven domains: visit history, medication burden, procedural utilisation, laboratory utilisation, composite clinical risk, medication-change patterns, and agerelated indicators; diagnosis codes were mapped into 16 clinically coherent categories.A hybrid stacking ensemble combining XGBoost, LightGBM and Extra Trees with a logistic-regression meta-learner was benchmarked against baseline classifiers.Performance was evaluated using accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, ROC-AUC and average precision (AP), while SHAP was used to interpret feature contributions.The hybrid stacking model achieved the highest ROC-AUC (0.7042), AP (0.6678), accuracy (0.6461) and precision (0.6377), whereas XGBoost achieved higher recall (0.6323) and F1-score (0.6246).The number of laboratory procedures, medication burden relative to length of stay (meds_per_day), total medication count, hospital duration, diagnostic categories and prior inpatient utilisation emerged as important predictors.The composite clinical_risk_score was higher among readmitted than non-readmitted encounters (mean 0.54 vs. 0.28), supporting its value as an interpretable risk representation.These findings indicate that clinically informed feature engineering can yield actionable and explainable predictors of diabetes readmission while showing that added ensemble complexity provides only marginal discrimination gains.External validation and prospective evaluation remain necessary before clinical deployment.

title: A NOISE-TOLERANT AND FIXED-TIME ZEROING NEURAL NETWORK MODEL FOR SOLVING MULTI-LINEAR $ \mathcal{M} $-TENSOR EQUATIONS
abstract: Zeroing neural network (ZNN) models are effective methods for solving multi-linear systems. To improve the performance of ZNN models, a new ZNN model is proposed for solving multi-linear systems with $ \mathcal{M} $-tensor in this paper. The proposed ZNN model incorporates with a nonlinear activation function. Convergence and robustness of the proposed ZNN model are analyzed. Theoretical results reveal that the proposed ZNN model converges within a fixed time and tolerates different types of noise. Numerical experiments illustrate that the proposed ZNN model is more powerful than some existing ZNN models for solving multi-linear systems with $ \mathcal{M} $-tensor.

title: What Makes a Good Fiqh Retriever? Answer Retrieval for Arabic Islamic Jurisprudence
abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation is used for Islamic question answering, but most systems are evaluated end-to-end, making retrieval failures difficult to isolate from generation failures. We study answer-bearing retrieval for Arabic fiqh, where a passage is relevant only if it states the ruling required by the question. We build a retrieval test collection for Arabic fiqh and use it to evaluate dense, lexical, hybrid, fine-tuned, and madhhab-aware retrieval strategies. The best retriever achieves 0.524 MRR@5, while fine-tuning improves performance to 0.553. Hybrid retrieval provides limited gains for strong models, whereas madhhab-aware filtering more than doubles MRR@5 on school-specific questions. We further present an error analysis showing that the main challenge is distinguishing answer-bearing passages from topically similar passages that do not contain the requested ruling.

title: Privacy-Preserving Detection of Rare Disease-Associated Cell Subsets via Secure Multi-Party Computation
abstract: The detection of rare disease-associated cell subsets from high-dimensional single-cell measurements is critical for understanding diseases such as leukaemia and viral infections. CellCnn, a convolutional neural network (CNN) designed for this task, has demonstrated the ability to identify phenotype-associated cell populations at frequencies as low as 0.01\%. Training such models reliably requires patient cohorts that are larger and more diverse than any single institution can typically assemble, and the underlying single-cell data is too sensitive to share across institutional boundaries under existing privacy regulations. We propose a secure multi-party computation (MPC) framework that enables the training and inference of CellCnn entirely on secret-shared data. This ensures that neither the participants nor the computing servers ever observe raw patient data or intermediate values. Evaluated on benchmark single-cell datasets for cytomegalovirus infection (CMV) and acute myeloid leukaemia (AML), our implementation preserves accuracy close to its plaintext counterpart while outperforming the prior privacy-preserving baseline. In contrast to earlier privacy-preserving approaches that removed components such as ReLU activations and bias terms, our method retains these key parts of the CellCnn architecture and supports accurate analysis without exposing raw patient data.

title: Rethinking the Evaluation and Optimization of LLM-Based Social Simulation
abstract: LLM-based social simulation is a promising complement to traditional methods such as surveys and behavioral experiments. A core question is how to evaluate the fidelity of LLM-simulated human behavior and optimize LLMs toward it. Prevailing practice evaluates by accuracy, checking whether the model selects the single response observed from a human, and trains the LLM to reproduce this hard label. However, human behavior is inherently subjective: the same person in the same situation may reasonably act differently, so an observed response is only one draw from an underlying response distribution, rendering accuracy-based evaluation unreliable and hard-label training misleading. To address these problems, we first introduce the subjectivity coefficient, an entropy-based quantity distinguishing objective tasks such as coding from subjective ones such as social simulation, and use it to systematically analyze how accuracy-based evaluation and hard-label training fail as subjectivity grows. Based on the subjectivity coefficient, we propose Subjectivity-Adaptive soft-Label Training (SALT): it pools observed outputs from semantically nearby inputs into soft distributional labels, with an aggregation radius adapted to the estimated subjectivity of each input; in the near-objective limit the neighborhood shrinks, so SALT naturally falls back to standard single-label training. Moreover, since existing datasets record only single observed responses and cannot support distributional evaluation, we construct SUBJSIM, a benchmark of 19,300 contexts covering 193 annotators and 100 subjective questions. Since real-world data typically provide only a single observation per input, our experiments train models from single observed outputs while evaluating them against the full response distributions, verifying feasibility in realistic settings. Results on SUBJSIM demonstrate the advantages of our method.

title: Optimal Unambiguous Dual-Rail Bell-State Measurement with Linear Optics and Two Ancillary Photons
abstract: Research package for the theorem that the optimal unambiguous dual-rail Bell-state measurement with static passive linear optics, ideal photon-number-resolving detection, and an arbitrary pure ancilla of exactly two photons has success probability exactly 3/4, with the general fixed-k bound (k+1)/(k+2) attained by the Grice hierarchy at k = 2^N - 2. Contains the manuscript (CC-BY 4.0), exact symbolic verification code with two independent amplitude engines, machine-readable certificates, and a kernel-checked Lean 4 certificate-layer formalization (MIT).

title: Algorithmic Substitution Invariance
abstract: This paper investigates the concept of algorithmic substitution invariance, a property where a replacement of a component within an algorithm maintains the same output, despite the change. We formally define this invariance using a notation where `C_i → C_i'` represents a substitution of component *C_i* with component *C_i'*, and we establish that invariance holds if `Output(C) = Output(C')`. Crucially, we introduce the metric `I_S(C_i)` to quantify the degree of invariance for a particular component *C_i*. This work lays the groundwork for understanding which substitutions are invariant under specific conditions, a fundamental challenge in algorithm verification and robustness analysis. The core contribution is a formalized framework for identifying and measuring algorithmic substitution invariance.

title: Algorithmic Necessity Measure
abstract: This paper introduces the concept of the Algorithmic Necessity Measure (ANM), a novel approach to evaluating the criticality of computational steps within a system. The ANM is defined as N(x), representing the loss of irreplaceable capability incurred by the removal of a specific computational step (x). This measure provides a rigorous distinction between optional, redundant, necessary, and core computations. The central aim is to establish Algorithmic Necessity Calculus, a formal framework for quantifying and managing computational criticality. This work lays the groundwork for more efficient and robust system design by prioritizing the preservation of essential computations, minimizing unnecessary complexity, and ultimately, improving overall system performance. The theoretical foundation presented here will be crucial for applications in diverse fields requiring precise control over computational processes, including complex simulation, optimization, and artificial intelligence.

title: DEVELOPMENT OF A SECURED DEEP LEARNING-BASED CARDIOVASCULAR DISEASE PREDICTION SYSTEM WITH ADVERSARIAL ATTACK DETECTION AND DEFENCE MECHANISMS
abstract: Cardiovascular disease (CVD) remains among the leading causes of mortality worldwide, and deep learning models are increasingly applied to ECG signals, medical imaging, and clinical records to support early detection and risk assessment. However, such models are known to be highly vulnerable to adversarial attacks, intentionally crafted, often imperceptible input perturbations that can force incorrect predictions and compromise patient safety. This study developed and evaluated a secured deep learning-based cardiovascular disease prediction system that integrates a predictive neural network with adversarial attack detection and defense mechanisms within a single pipeline. Statistical anomaly detection, autoencoder-based reconstruction error analysis, and input sensitivity evaluation were combined to flag manipulated inputs, while adversarial training, input preprocessing, and ensemble-based regularization were used to strengthen model resilience. The system was benchmarked on standard datasets and evaluated under Fast Gradient Sign Method (FGSM), Projected Gradient Descent (PGD), and Carlini & Wagner (C&W) attack simulations. Results show that although the baseline model achieved strong performance on clean data (96.4% accuracy), performance degraded substantially under adversarial conditions in the absence of protection, most severely under PGD attack. Integrating detection and defense mechanisms raised adversarial accuracy from 58.7% to 88.6% while preserving clean-data performance, confirming that a layered, security-first architecture meaningfully improves the reliability and trustworthiness of AI-driven cardiovascular prediction systems without materially sacrificing predictive accuracy.

title: Semantic Temperature Field
abstract: This paper introduces the concept of a Semantic Temperature Field (STF), a novel framework for understanding and managing knowledge representation and adaptation in dynamic learning environments. Unlike traditional approaches rooted in thermodynamics, the STF utilizes a 'temperature' metric to quantify the stability and malleability of knowledge within defined semantic regions. High temperature signifies regions prone to rapid change, while low temperature indicates extreme stability. The STF provides a unified mechanism for addressing continuous learning, forgetting, and fine-tuning processes, offering a potentially more nuanced and effective approach to knowledge management compared to existing methods. The core of the STF revolves around the dynamic adjustment of these temperature values to govern the learning and retention processes within a system. This paper lays out the foundational principles of the STF and discusses its potential applications.

title: Engineering Secure AI Systems with Lattice-Based Cryptography and Large Language Models
abstract: Deploying large language models in safety-critical domains while migrating to post-quantum cryptographic standards poses a compounded systems engineering challenge: infrastructure must become privacy-preserving, computa-tionally viable, and quantum-resistant at once. This review examines three frontiers where lattice-based cryptography and large language models converge, applying an evidence-grading scheme that separates established results from conjecture. The first frontier is fully homomorphic encryption for private model training. Ciphertext error does not provide differential privacy: it is not calibrated to query sensitivity, involves no gradient clipping, and is removed by decryption. The two mechanisms defend against disjoint adversaries and must be composed, not substituted. The second frontier is the hypothesis that language models can act as adaptive agents inside lattice reduction. No empirical result supports it. The review further shows that scheduling improvements cannot reduce core security estimates, since these depend on the minimum viable block size rather than the number of reduction tours, and supplies a falsifiable benchmark protocol in place of the parameter-selection guidance of earlier treatments. The third frontier is functional encryption for decentralized inference. Inner-product constructions admit exact reconstruction of hidden states by any node holding a spanning key set, requiring no cryptanalysis, so security rests on key allocation rather than lattice hardness. Attention is bilinear and lies outside the inner-product functionality class. Quantitatively, encrypted inference for a small encoder costs roughly five orders of magnitude more than plaintext, measured on a graphics processing unit; functional key material reaches four tebibytes per attention layer under the parameters the security proof requires, reducible by three orders of magnitude at a stated security cost; and memory capacity, not arithmetic throughput, is the binding constraint. evidence.title: Engineering Secure AI Systems with Lattice-Based Cryptography and Large Language Models
evidence.abstract: Deploying large language models in safety-critical domains while migrating to post-quantum cryptographic standards poses a compounded systems engineering challenge: infrastructure must become privacy-preserving, computa-tionally viable, and quantum-resistant at once. This review examines three frontiers where lattice-based cryptography and large language models converge, applying an evidence-grading scheme that separates established results from conjecture. The first frontier is fully homomorphic encryption for private model training. Ciphertext error does not provide differential privacy: it is not calibrated to query sensitivity, involves no gradient clipping, and is removed by decryption. The two mechanisms defend against disjoint adversaries and must be composed, not substituted. The second frontier is the hypothesis that language models can act as adaptive agents inside lattice reduction. No empirical result supports it. The review further shows that scheduling improvements cannot reduce core security estimates, since these depend on the minimum viable block size rather than the number of reduction tours, and supplies a falsifiable benchmark protocol in place of the parameter-selection guidance of earlier treatments. The third frontier is functional encryption for decentralized inference. Inner-product constructions admit exact reconstruction of hidden states by any node holding a spanning key set, requiring no cryptanalysis, so security rests on key allocation rather than lattice hardness. Attention is bilinear and lies outside the inner-product functionality class. Quantitatively, encrypted inference for a small encoder costs roughly five orders of magnitude more than plaintext, measured on a graphics processing unit; functional key material reaches four tebibytes per attention layer under the parameters the security proof requires, reducible by three orders of magnitude at a stated security cost; and memory capacity, not arithmetic throughput, is the binding constraint. Readiness levels for the three frontiers span one to three. Trusted execution environments remain the only approach in production today.

title: A Formal Framework of Architectural Intent Collapse for Tool-Level Attacks on LLM Agents
abstract: Tool-level attacks on Large Language Model (LLM) agents—poisoned tool descriptions, prompt injection, and capability misrepresentation—are universally effective, yet no existing defense provides comprehensive protection. We propose Architectural Intent Collapse (AIC), a formal framework capturing the systematic loss of communicative intent when text from heterogeneous sources is flattened into a single context window. Grounded as a novel instantiation of the Confused Deputy Problem, AIC reveals that the missing boundary is not permission but intent: the architecture cannot distinguish descriptive statements from prescriptive commands. We formalize AIC via an architectural collapse operator, introduce Intent Separation Degree (ISD) as a measurable metric, and develop a mechanism-based taxonomy of five intent-disguise attack types, including two previously undescribed (Conditional Latency and Inference Inducement). Experiments across 25 framework–model combinations (employing GPT-4o, Claude-4-Sonnet, Gemini-2.5-Pro, DeepSeek-V3, and Qwen3-32B as LLM backends) confirm that ISD degrades with description verbosity, strongly predicts defense effectiveness (r=−0.97), and is uniformly low across all current frameworks. Three root-cause defense principles are derived; one retains substantial protection against adaptive attackers. This research is useful for agent framework designers, security practitioners, and researchers seeking a principled understanding of why tool-level attacks succeed and how architectural defenses can address their root cause.

title: InsufficiencyBench: Evaluating LLM legal advice on underspecified user queries
abstract: Legal AI systems are increasingly used to answer legal questions, yet existing benchmarks assume queries arrive fully specified. In practice, users omit facts that materially determine the legal outcome. We introduce InsufficiencyBench, the first legal benchmark targeting query-side insufficiency: whether a model recognizes when a query lacks legally material information, identifies what is missing, and refrains from premature conclusions. We formalize a taxonomy of eight canonical missing-element categories across three structural failure modes---switch, gating, and fatal prerequisite--- and construct 202 benchmark items (58 base queries, 144 deficient variants) spanning six legal domains and 24 US jurisdictions and annotated by practising attorneys. Evaluating ten frontier models, we find that no model exceeds F2 = 0.46 on missing-element identification and that the median recall is 0.44. Models either hedge indiscriminately or answer silently under fabricated presumptions. No model both identifies and qualifies responses to deficient queries while directly addressing complete ones.

title: Entangling two qudits of arbitrary dimension through light-atomic Faraday interaction
abstract: The paper investigates entangling operations acting on two qudits of arbitrary dimension, with one encoded in the states of a spatially multimode optical field, the other in those of atomic collective spin coherence, both carrying orbital angular momentum (OAM). We demonstrate the generation of a wide range of entangling operations within a protocol consisting of two Faraday interactions and a rotation of atomic and light quadratures between them. All generated gates can be represented as rational powers of the d-dimensional gate $SWAP^α_d$. The probabilities of two-qudit transformations are calculated for various dimensions of the logical space and for different entangling powers of the logical gates.

title: Towards Benchmarking Agentic Data Scientists
abstract: Agentic machine learning systems leverage large language models to autonomously design, execute, and refine machine learning pipelines. Despite rapid progress in this area, systematic evaluation of these systems remains limited. In this work, we benchmark four representative approaches: MLZero, AgentK, AIDE, and an open-source reimplementation of MLE-STAR. Additionally, we use AutoGluon as an AutoML baseline. We use a unified evaluation framework with fixed data splits and standardized metrics. Beyond predictive performance, we evaluate execution reliability, robustness, and failure behavior. Our results show that ensemble-based systems such as AutoGluon provide the most stable and consistent performance across heterogeneous tasks, while agentic approaches occasionally achieve strong task-specific results but exhibit higher variance and frequent execution failures. The study highlights important trade-offs between reasoning-based automation, robustness, and practical usability, and provides a reproducible benchmark for future research on agentic machine learning systems. Codebase available at https://github.com/KARTIK-N-NAYAK/Benchmarking-Agentic-Data-Scientists

title: Computational Realization of Conservation
abstract: This paper investigates the concept of computational conservation, exploring how algorithms can be designed to preserve specific invariants despite transformations. The central argument posits that the invariance of a system's real representation (Ireal) is a more fundamental concept than the invariance of the underlying program itself. We introduce a framework for identifying and realizing these invariant representations, focusing on the transformation [P → Q] and the preservation of the real invariants [Ireal(P) = Ireal(Q)]. The paper illustrates this with an example of a potential invariant function representation, highlighting the distinction between algorithmic and real invariance. This work lays the groundwork for a deeper understanding of how computational systems can guarantee conservation properties, particularly in complex and evolving environments.

title: Algorithmic Layer Irreducibility
abstract: This paper investigates the concept of algorithmic layer irreducibility, proposing a framework for understanding situations where a high-level algorithmic description fundamentally differs from its low-level implementation, even when the low-level implementation ultimately realizes the high-level functionality. We explore conditions under which this irreducibility manifests, suggesting it represents a novel form of abstraction irreducibility beyond simple implementation differences. The core argument centers around the divergence of logical representations and the potential for inherent information loss or gain during the translation process. The paper defines key terms, outlines a theoretical model, and discusses implications for algorithm design, verification, and understanding complex systems. We present a formalization of the concept and explore its relationship to other related areas such as program equivalence and abstraction hierarchies.

title: Algorithmic Direction Invariant
abstract: This paper investigates the concept of an algorithmic direction invariant, a core property determining the inherent robustness of a computational process against transformations such as compilation, reordering, optimization, parallelization, and other manipulations. The central question addressed is: What constitutes a truly irreversible directional information within an algorithm? We introduce a framework for identifying and quantifying this invariant, denoted as *ID(C)*, where *C* represents a computational sequence. The framework posits that the directionality of a computation, characterized by the sequence of states [ *x0*, *x1*, ..., *xn* ], can be preserved through various algorithmic stages, forming an invariant structure. The paper outlines a method for detecting this invariant and explores the implications for algorithm design and analysis, particularly concerning the preservation of algorithmic flow and dependencies. The theoretical underpinnings are discussed, focusing on the relationship between algorithmic structure, computational transformations, and the persistent directional information. We propose a formal definition of *ID(C)* and its relation to key algorithmic properties.

title: Computational Null Structure
abstract: This paper introduces the Null Structure Theory, a novel approach to understanding and identifying fundamental limitations within computational systems. The core premise is that the absence of a particular structure is often more significant than its presence. Rather than focusing on the existence of elements, this theory centers on demonstrating the *non-existence* of structures that *must* be null. This is achieved through a formalized computational framework, utilizing specific mathematical operations and notation to rigorously define and test for these null conditions. The theoretical underpinnings are presented, alongside a set of guiding principles for constructing and evaluating systems designed to exploit these null structures. The ultimate goal is to shift the focus from simply building complex systems to proactively eliminating potentially problematic structures, leading to more robust, reliable, and efficient computational designs. The investigation is predicated on the idea that identifying and preventing the formation of null structures is a critical step in avoiding unexpected behavior and ensuring the integrity of the computational process. The presented methodology offers a new lens through which to approach system design and analysis.

title: A general view-factor based irradiation distribution model for multi-row bifacial PV arrays on sloped and reflective ground
abstract: We present a view-factor based model to calculate the irradiation distribution on the front- and backside of a photovoltaic panel in a multi-row array on arbitrarily sloped ground. This allows us to accurately assess the performance of high-alpine photovoltaic plants that are built on sloped terrain, and further allows the assessment of irradiation inhomogeneity on the panel surface which can be useful for the calculation of mismatch losses. The model is validated against an experimental and automatically adjustable miniature-PV plant located at the Totalp site in Davos (CH), which enables the systematic evaluation across a variety of array configurations. For most configurations and both sides of the panels, the deviations are within 5 %, with neglected direct panel reflection most likely accounting for a majority of the model-side errors. The model application is showcased by quantifying the inhomogeneity of backside irradiation in a specific case and by comparing the yearly irradiation of different arrays with equal shading angles, both highlighting the need for a generally applicable model.

title: QUASAR: A Quantum-Classical Neural Network for SAR Satellite Physical-Layer Authentication
abstract: X-band SAR satellites (8-12 GHz) play a critical role in disaster response, environmental monitoring, and military intelligence. Yet, they lack robust physical-layer authentication (PLA), a security layer orthogonal to cryptographic solutions. Existing PLA systems, typically based on radio-frequency fingerprinting, are often limited to sub-6 GHz frequencies and rely on classical deep learning. However, this approach underfits the IQ phase nonlinearities that distinguish satellite hardware. In this paper, we present QUASAR, to the best of our knowledge the first quantum-classical hybrid architecture that fuses a CNN spectrogram encoder with a variational quantum circuit (VQC) to provide PLA to X-band SAR signals. Our solution enjoys two distinctive features: (i) it is markedly more data-efficient than classical machine learning, requiring only 10% of the training data to match the accuracy of classical baselines -- data collection being notoriously the most time-consuming phase of PLA; and, (ii) at an equal data budget, it improves classification accuracy over those baselines. In detail, we test our solution under three adversarial scenarios: replay, crafted-IQ injection, and space-borne spoofing. QUASAR rejects spoofed transmissions in 89.7%, 94.1%, and 81.3% of attempts, respectively, establishing the first quantum-enhanced physical-layer classifier for satellite constellations. The fully detailed framework and the supporting results, other than being interesting on their own, show a novel research avenue for physical-layer authentication.

title: Recursive Category Theory
abstract: Recursive Category Theory (RCT) proposes a framework in which the notion of a category is extended to include the entire category of categories as an object, thereby enabling an infinite recursion of categorical structures. This paper develops the core definitions of RCT, constructs a recursive universe of categories, and investigates its fundamental properties. By treating each category as a self-similar object, we establish a hierarchy of levels where each level contains the previous as a substructure. We provide examples illustrating how familiar categorical concepts such as functors, natural transformations, and limits can be interpreted within this recursive setting. The implications for mathematical foundations, logic, and theoretical computer science are discussed, with an emphasis on the potential for a unified approach to higher-dimensional and higher-order categorical phenomena.

By treating each category as a self-similar object, we establish a hierarchy of levels where each level contains the previous as a substructure. We provide examples illustrating how familiar categorical concepts such as functors, natural transformations, and limits can be interpreted within this recursive setting. The implications for mathematical foundations, logic, and theoretical computer science are discussed, with an emphasis on the potential for a unified approach to higher-dimensional and higher-order categorical phenomena.

title: Algorithmic Rigidity Theory
abstract: Algorithmic Rigidity Theory (ART) introduces a novel framework for analyzing the difficulty of optimization problems, moving beyond traditional notions of stability. ART focuses on the structural immutability of a solution, defining rigidity as the resistance of a solution to changes in its underlying algorithmic representation. Higher rigidity implies greater difficulty in optimization due to the inherent constraints imposed by the problem's structure. This theory provides a new lens through which to understand optimization challenges, particularly in complex systems where subtle algorithmic variations can drastically impact solution quality. The core concept is represented mathematically as follows: Let *S* be a solution to an optimization problem *P*, and let *A* represent the algorithmic representation of *P*. Rigidity, denoted by *R(S, A)*, is defined as: *R(S, A) = max{ α }* Where α represents the sensitivity of the solution *S* to changes in *A*. This sensitivity is quantified by the maximum change in the objective function value, *f(S)*, that results from a permissible modification of *A*. A higher *R(S, A)* indicates a more rigid solution, and consequently, a more challenging optimization problem. The theory posits that rigidity is not merely a measure of stability, but a fundamentally different property reflecting the inherent structure of the solution. This framework allows for a more nuanced and accurate assessment of optimization problem difficulty.

title: Smart Comment Manager: Streamlining Comment Analysis and Viewer Query Clustering Using NLP Processing
abstract: In Today’s world, YouTube and other content creators are frequently barraged by a deluge of spam, unrelated remarks, and even hate messages, which makes it challenging for them to have a healthy and active online community. The more their audience, the more time-consuming are the traditional moderation practices and the less insight the audience opinion provides. This disconnection renders the creators incapable of knowing and redressing the problems of their community. Adding to the problem are the fuzzy logic limitations in identifying subtle topics and emotive cues, where misinterpretation can diminish the strength of content analysis. To fill these gaps, the NLP-driven Smart Comment Manager is set to simplify and enhance comment analysis. The platform is made user-friendly and removes hate speech, spam, and clusters duplicate questions, allowing creators to respond better and build a better and more engaging community. This system is built from three foundation modules: Hate Speech and Spam Detection, with RoBERTA to detect toxic content quickly and efficiently; Similar Question Clustering, with stsb-distilbert-base, to cluster repetitive questions for best responses; and Topic Discovery, with BERTopic, to detect trending topics in both comment streams and live chat. Smart Comment Manager converts comment streams into active feedback engines for building audience engagement and community, not passive feedback pipelines. Beyond content creation, the platform is also beneficial to customer support teams and online communities where handling massive amounts of user feedback is critical.

title: Drill-Core SWIR-Based 3D Alteration Modeling and Machine Learning for Gold Prospectivity Prediction at the Tudui–Shawang Gold Deposit, Jiaodong Peninsula
abstract: Deep exploration in mature gold districts requires subsurface alteration evidence that can be related quantitatively to three-dimensional (3D) geological architecture. This study develops a workflow for the Tudui–Shawang deposit in the Muping–Rushan metallogenic belt that integrates drill-core short-wave infrared (SWIR) spectroscopy, 3D alteration modeling, ore-controlling geological constraints, positive–unlabeled (PU) learning, and ensemble prospectivity prediction. A total of 2140 spectra from 10 drillholes were processed to identify mineral assemblages, extract spectral scalars and feature-shape attributes, classify alteration facies, and construct continuous 3D alteration evidence. Discrete smooth interpolation and indicator kriging were used for continuous and categorical attributes, respectively, and CatBoost, LightGBM, XGBoost, and Random Forest were evaluated within a spatially separated PU-bagging design. Quantitative analyses show that individual SWIR attributes have weak deposit-scale relationships with Au grade. Nevertheless, local IC minima, relatively lower pos2200 values near several mineralized intervals, alteration-facies transitions, and a broader shift toward longer pos2250 wavelengths characterize relevant parts of the mineralized system. FUSE performed best under 1 km × 1 km spatial holdout validation, with an ROC AUC of 0.8900 and a PRAUC of 0.8926. Prediction-area analysis and the 3D probability volume delineated three ranked exploration targets (T1–T3). The results show that drill-core SWIR-derived 3D alteration evidence, when integrated with ore-controlling geology and spatially validated machine learning, provides a practical basis for target prioritization in mature gold districts.

title: Когнитивное исследование производства риса в краснодарском крае
authors: международная научно-практическая конференция (28; 2024; Санкт-Петербург) "Системный анализ в проектировании и управлении"
abstract: Рис является одним из важнейших сельскохозяйственных продуктов, определяющих продовольственную безопасность страны. Краснодарский край – это основной рисосеющий регион России. Эффективность этой отрасли зависит не только от благоприятных условий края, но и от применяемых агротехнологий и правильного водопользования. В статье изложены некоторые результаты когнитивного имитационного моделирования системы производства риса, проведенного с целью разработки сценариев развития производства в разных природных и экономических условиях и оценки влияния разных агроприемов. Приводится разработанная когнитивная карта и несколько сценариев развития рисоводства.

title: ContractScrub: A benchmark for final review of legal contracts
abstract: Legal work, with its heavy reliance on processing large amounts of text, is often considered one of the domains most exposed to the use of LLMs. Contract ``scrubbing,'' the final review of transactional agreements for errors and inconsistencies, is a particularly suitable task for automation, because it is routine, painstaking work requiring detailed attention to long documents. Scrubbing also seems to align naturally with the general capabilities expected of frontier LLMs around long-context reasoning, consistency checking, and named entity recognition (NER). Despite the economic value and potential for automation, no formal evaluations of LLMs performing contract scrubbing have been conducted. We introduce ContractScrub, the first benchmark designed to evaluate contract scrubbing capabilities, comprising contracts hand-crafted by experienced lawyers over diverse error categories such as misuse of defined terms, incorrect references, and inconsistent language. Frontier models perform surprisingly poorly with only one model reaching 0.75 macro average recall despite strong performance on seemingly related general benchmarks, demonstrating the practical limits of current models and the importance of narrowly targeted, domain-specific benchmarks for measuring real-world impact.

title: AI strategic embeddedness and the contingent value of artificial intelligence in organisations
abstract: Firms making comparable investments in artificial intelligence can realise very different strategic returns. Existing research explains AI capability, managerial cognition, human-AI work design and governance largely in separate streams, leaving unresolved how AI’s position inside organisational decision architecture conditions the value it produces. Why does AI change what some organisations are able to decide and do, while remaining a productivity tool at the edge of others? This paper develops the construct of AI strategic embeddedness, defined as the configuration of four placements through which AI systems become constitutive of an organisation’s attention structures, decision routines, work arrangements and learning processes rather than adjacent to them. Drawing on dynamic capabilities, the attention-based view and research on human-AI complementarity, we specify four mechanisms through which embeddedness produces value. These are attention reallocation, routine reconfiguration, complementarity in judgement and recursive learning. We then theorise four features that existing accounts miss. The attention mechanism expands the signals an organisation sees while confining them to the region its models represent. Governance conditions that value through an adequacy threshold and a burden gradient, so value is lower below a minimum standard of governance adequacy, and returns to further procedural burden above it diminish and eventually turn negative. Embeddedness contains a corroding loop in which sustained reliance erodes the human expertise that the complementarity mechanism requires, which we call the capability-dependence paradox. And embeddedness built on widely shared general-purpose models compresses the dispersion of strategic issue framing between firms, while raising absolute decision quality only where the models are well fitted to the task, so private value can rise without relative advantage. Ten numbered propositions, with Proposition 8 divided into two linked predictions, and a research agenda follow from the framework. The last of them concerns how domain-level embeddedness aggregates to the firm.

title: Security Architecture for AI Agent Systems
abstract: Large Language Model agents that call external tools are vulnerable to indirect prompt injection: adversarial instructions hidden in retrieved data can hijack the agent into unauthorised tool calls or data exfiltration. CaMeL (Google DeepMind, 2025), the foundational system-level defence, separates a Privileged LLM that never sees untrusted data from a Quarantined LLM that cannot call tools, and enforces capability-based taint tracking to reduce attack success to zero by design. But its guarantee assumes untrusted data never influences control flow — an assumption broken by common tasks such as triaging emails or routing queries, where which tool to call depends on data the planner has not yet seen. This thesis extends system-level defences to such data-dependent control flow and maps their limits. It reproduces CaMeL on AgentDojo with Claude Sonnet 4 (77.5% utility, 0% attack success across 560 attacks); presents a multi-label decomposition of 640 runs isolating data-dependent control flow as the largest irreducible architectural residue; and develops a four-category taxonomy (DDC-1 to DDC-4) with an explicit solvability boundary. It then proposes scope-guarded branching: the planner declares a fixed set of branches and per-branch tool scopes before any untrusted data is read, and a quarantined classifier selects among them without widening the action set. Across 240 adversarial runs, no tool call ever escaped the pre-declared scope, even at a 54–65% classifier-flip rate. The central principle is that security should rest not on the classifier's robustness, but on what the surrounding architecture statically constrains it to do.

title: Information Encounter Algebra
abstract: This paper introduces Information Encounter Algebra (IEA), a novel algebraic structure proposed to formalize the process of encountering information. The core concept revolves around the "encounter" operation, denoted as '\star', which represents the interaction and fusion of two information structures. This work investigates the fundamental properties of this operation, specifically whether the associative property holds for the encounter operation applied to multiple structures. The investigation demonstrates that the encounter operation is not necessarily associative, leading to the conclusion that information encounter possesses an inherent algebraic structure. This finding suggests the potential development of a comprehensive mathematical framework for analyzing and manipulating information encounters, offering new tools for understanding complex information systems. The paper outlines the foundational concepts and presents the initial algebraic formalism of IEA, focusing on the encounter operation and its implications. ---

title: Exploring the Utilisation of AI among Professionals in Advertising Agencies in Lagos, Nigeria
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) continues to redefine global culture, the economy, politics, and professional practice, including advertising. Nigeria’s advertising industry aligns closely with global trends and professional standards. This chapter explores the use of AI among professionals working in advertising agencies in Lagos, Nigeria. It investigates the level of awareness and adoption of AI among agency operators, identifies prominent AI tools used in advertising practice, and examines the ethical challenges associated with their use. Drawing on Diffusion of Innovation Theory and Technology Acceptance Theory, this study adopts a descriptive survey design using questionnaires to address key research questions. In a 2024 survey conducted by the researchers, 153 advertising agency professionals participated. Findings show that 92.2% of respondents demonstrate awareness of AI-related issues. About 52.9% believe AI currently sits within the early adoption phase in Nigeria. Practitioners reported improved efficiency, streamlined operations, creative optimisation, and automation as key benefits. However, concerns about intellectual theft and data privacy remain significant ethical challenges.

title: PLAI: A Pilot Study of Profile-Based Explanation for AI-Supported Learning
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as on-demand conversational learning assistants, but they typically do not adapt explanations to a student’s background unless explicitly prompted. We present the Personalized Learning Assistant Interface (PLAI), a web-based prototype that generates explanations from lecture slides, audio transcripts, and a structured student profile through a chat-based interface. We evaluated PLAI in a controlled pilot study with 24 STEM students, comparing profile-based personalization with a baseline condition using the same slide and transcript context. Immediate learning was assessed with a five-item knowledge test, while subjective experience was measured using the User Experience Questionnaire (UEQ) and open-ended feedback. We did not observe clear differences in knowledge-test outcomes, but participants in the personalized condition reported significantly higher UEQ Stimulation. These results suggest that profile-based multimodal prompts may mainly support motivational engagement rather than immediate test performance, while larger and longer-term studies are needed to assess learning effects.

title: Dynamic Gated Cross-Modal Fusion with Sarcastic-aware Contrastive Regularization for Multimodal Sarcasm Detection
abstract: Multimodal sarcasm detection aims to identify sarcastic intent from multimodal content, where inconsistencies between literal meaning and contextual cues often signal irony. This task has attracted increasing research attention. However, accurate detection remains challenging due to instance-dependent modality contributions and misleading semantic consistency, where surface-level alignment masks underlying contradictory intent. Existing methods often rely on fixed fusion strategies and treat sarcasm as generic cross-modal mismatch, limiting their ability to capture subtle sarcasm cues and instance-specific modality interactions. To address these challenges, we propose a novel MSD framework that integrates Dynamic Gated Cross-Modal Fusion with Sarcastic-aware Contrastive Regularization (SaCR). Specifically, a bidirectional gated interaction module performs cross-modal feature filtering and adaptively calibrates textual and visual contributions at the instance level. A dynamic fusion gate further balances modality importance to generate more robust multimodal representations. Furthermore, SaCR is introduced as a label-aware contrastive regularization objective that encourages semantic consistency for non-sarcastic samples while suppressing misleading consistency in sarcastic cases. The proposed framework is trained end-to-end with a multi-objective learning strategy that jointly optimizes multimodal classification and auxiliary unimodal supervision. Extensive experiments on MMSD and MMSD2.0 demonstrate that the proposed method consistently outperforms strong baselines.

title: Securing Filesystems for Confidential Computing
abstract: Confidential computing protects applications inside Trusted Execution Environments (TEEs), but it leaves storage vulnerable. Even with disk encryption, a malicious cloud provider can roll back, replay, fork, or tamper with disk state, breaking the integrity and freshness guarantees required by stateful applications. Existing solutions either assume trusted storage, incur high overheads, or push integrity logic into applications. We present ShieldFS, a POSIX-compliant filesystem that provides end-to-end integrity and freshness for persistent storage in the confidential-computing threat model without requiring application changes. ShieldFS represents permissible filesystem states using succinct cryptographic commitments, maintained inside TEEs and replicated in a lightweight trusted registry. On-disk data structures, including a write-ahead log and a storage pool, are authenticated using hash chains and an embedded Merkle tree. ShieldFS utilizes transactions and copy-on-write to update persistent filesystem state and commitments atomically. The commitments are verified during reads, ensuring that rollback, replay, and equivocation attacks are detected even when the entire I/O stack is untrusted. We implement the design by extending ZFS, yielding ShieldZFS. Evaluation with standard filesystem benchmarks and real-world workloads shows that ShieldZFS provides strong integrity and freshness guarantees with performance comparable to state-of-the-art filesystems.

ShieldFS utilizes transactions and copy-on-write to update persistent filesystem state and commitments atomically. The commitments are verified during reads, ensuring that rollback, replay, and equivocation attacks are detected even when the entire I/O stack is untrusted. We implement the design by extending ZFS, yielding ShieldZFS. Evaluation with standard filesystem benchmarks and real-world workloads shows that ShieldZFS provides strong integrity and freshness guarantees with performance comparable to state-of-the-art filesystems.

title: Differential Privacy in Feature Reconstruction Aided Federated Learning for Agent's Semantic Communication Model Update
abstract: This paper proposes a differentially private federated learning (FL) framework built upon an FL algorithm with semantic feature reconstruction (FedSFR) for training semantic communication modules for image transmission. By allowing clients with unfavorable uplink capacity to transmit low-dimensional semantic feature vectors extracted from locally trained joint source-channel coding (JSCC) encoders, FedSFR enhances communication efficiency and training stability under heterogeneous wireless conditions. To protect client privacy, we incorporate the oneshot Laplace mechanism and theoretically demonstrate that feature-based transmission achieves strictly stronger differential privacy (DP) guarantees than gradient-based transmission under an identical communication budget. In addition, a model selection mechanism is introduced to alleviate performance degradation caused by privacy-preserving perturbations. Experimental results on multiple datasets show that the proposed DP-aided FedSFR outperforms DP-enabled FedAvg in training stability and image reconstruction quality in heterogeneous wireless systems.

title: Machine competence or human experience? A source-task congruence framework for AI-generated travel recommendations
abstract: Travelers can now receive advice from generative artificial intelligence alongside human experts, peers and review platforms, yet prior research reports AI aversion, AI appreciation and source parity under different conditions. This conceptual paper develops a source-task congruence framework to explain when AI-attributed travel recommendations are more or less persuasive and specifies the observations that would reject the framework. It integrates source credibility theory, research on testimony and epistemic vigilance, mind perception research, tourism authenticity scholarship and work on algorithm aversion and appreciation. The framework distinguishes epistemic credibility, defined as source expertise in the credibility literature, from experiential credibility, a source-level judgment of perceived direct acquaintance with the focal place. It proposes that source attribution affects the perceived level of each credibility currency, while recommendation task warrant determines the diagnostic weight assigned to each during trust formation. Informational tasks are proposed to weight epistemic credibility more heavily, whereas experiential tasks weight experiential credibility more heavily, so persuasion depends on the match between the credibility currency a source is perceived to hold and that required by the task. Capability-enhancing information is predicted to narrow the AI-human gap more for informational than experiential tasks, providing a discriminating test against purely ability-based explanations. The paper develops eight propositions and a six-study validation agenda with prespecified effect thresholds. It also identifies the confounding of human identity with direct visitation, specifies a four-condition design to separate them, and outlines the measurement work required before testing two central variables. Conditional on empirical support, the framework implies that source labeling may carry different credibility consequences depending on whether it signals direct visitation or generic editorial oversight. The paper defines experiential credibility as a source judgment, introduces recommendation task warrant as distinct from subjectivity and hedonicity, and specifies tests separating source-task congruence from ability, originality, anthropomorphism- and human-favoritism-based accounts. All propositions remain untested.

title: Algorithmic Layer Equivalence
abstract: This paper investigates the concept of algorithmic layer equivalence, proposing a novel equivalence relation between two software systems despite their fundamentally different internal implementations. The core argument posits that if two systems share the same abstract layer structure, they should be considered equivalent. This contrasts with traditional notions of program equivalence and function equivalence, which focus on identical execution behavior. We define this equivalence using a layer-centric approach, emphasizing the shared logical organization of the systems. The paper explores the implications of this equivalence relation for software verification, testing, and maintenance, suggesting it can provide a more efficient and practical approach than focusing solely on low-level implementation details. We present a formal framework for defining and evaluating algorithmic layer equivalence, utilizing mathematical notation to clearly articulate the concepts and relationships involved. The investigation highlights the potential of this equivalence relation to simplify software development and improve the overall understanding of complex systems. ---

title: Semantic Causation Theory
abstract: This paper introduces the Semantic Causation Theory (SCT), a novel framework proposing that causal relationships extend beyond the realm of variables to encompass semantic concepts. Traditional causality focuses on relationships between measurable variables, while SCT posits that a semantic shift – a change in understanding or interpretation – can itself be a cause. The theory is built upon the concept of Semantic Causal Operators (SCOs), which define the mechanisms through which semantic causation occurs. This work outlines the core tenets of SCT, exploring the nature of SCOs and providing a preliminary model for understanding how semantic changes can initiate or influence other semantic changes. The theoretical framework presented aims to broaden our understanding of causality and provide a new lens through which to analyze phenomena involving conceptual shifts and meaning evolution.

title: TexNet: A Statewide Seismic Monitoring Network as Geographic Information Infrastructure
abstract: Seismic monitoring networks increasingly develop capabilities that function as geographic information infrastructure, transforming continuous geophysical observations into spatial information that supports research, decision-making, and public awareness. In Texas, seismicity linked to oil and gas operations has increased since 2009 across major producing regions, prompting the Texas Legislature to establish the Texas Seismological Network and Seismology Research program (TexNet) in 2015. This paper examines TexNet’s seismic monitoring network, field operations, data-processing pipeline, and the information products, data services, and decision-support tools that transform seismic observations into accessible earthquake information. Since routine earthquake reporting began in 2017, TexNet has grown from an inherited network of eighteen broadband stations to a system directly maintaining 207 stations and incorporating 421 active stations to locate earthquakes across Texas. TexNet provides a suite of information products, data services, and decision-support tools—including the TexNet Earthquake Catalog, near-real-time notification systems, and open data products—that connect geophysical observations with the needs of researchers, regulatory agencies, industry, and the public. TexNet remains fundamentally a seismic monitoring network, with additional capabilities that support scientific, regulatory, and public information needs in Texas and other regions with induced seismicity.

title: Effects of Interaction Modality on LLM-Based Information-Seeking
abstract: Conversational Large Language Models (LLMs), increasingly also in voice mode, are reshaping how people seek and engage with information. Understanding modality effects on interaction patterns and user perspectives is essential for interaction design that balances factors such as trust, usability, and user experience. This paper presents a within-subject experiment (n = 33) comparing how text, voice, and mixed-modality interaction influence LLM-based information search, with participants composing recommendations in health-related scenarios. We find that voice-based and mixed-modality interactions were characterized by a more conversational interaction style, with higher turn ratios, more frequent follow-up questions, and shorter responses than text mode. User experience evaluations indicated differences in hedonic quality, but not in pragmatic quality. We observed no differences in the quality of participants’ recommendations, perceived cognitive load, trust, and anthropomorphism. Qualitative findings highlight situation-dependent preferences. We recommend that LLM-based search systems support mixed interaction modalities that allow for adjustment to preferences and task demands.
